passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The Republic of Maldives is an island country in the Indian Ocean.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: It has 1199 ands that are clustered into 26 major atolls.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef or a string of closely spaced coral islands.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The natural coral reefs of Maldives surrounded by lagoons make each island stand out as a pearl in the Indian Ocean.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The Maldives stands at eighth position amongst the smallest countries in the world with an area of 300 square kilometres only.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: It is the smallest Asian country with respect to population size.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: people have been living on the islands of the Maldives from as long as 3000 years.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: They set sail from different parts of the world- Asia, Arabia, Europe and the Americas- to come to these islands.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The earliest settlers of the Maldives were probably from southern India and Sri Lanka who came to these islands in the fourth fifth centuries BC.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: In the 12th century AD, sailors from East Africa and Arab countries came to the Maldives.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: As a result, the Maldivians who were originally Buddhists were converted to Sunni

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: Islam in the mid-12th century.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: In 1344 Ibn Batuta, a famous :Arab historian and scholar travelled around the Maldives.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: In the 16th century, the Portuguese conquered the Maldives and they ruled the country for 15 years.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: Although governed as an independent Islamic sultanate for most of its history from 1153 to 1968, the Maldives was a British colony from 1887 to 1965.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: Following independence from Britain in 1965, the sultanate continued to operate for another 3 years.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: On November 11, 1968, it was abolished and replaced by a republic and the country assumed its present name.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The Maldives is famous as a tourist destination because of its enjoyable weather, heavenly beaches and lagoons, luxurious holiday resorts and the peace-loving people.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: Being an island country, it enjoys a pleasant weather throughout the year.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The Maldives has been ranked as the best country brand for beach, rest and relaxation in 2008.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: In the same year, it was also ranked second as the best country brand for natural beauty.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The Maldives is well known for being the lowest country in the world.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: Unfortunately, this small country with idyllic natural beauty is under threat from rising sea levels due to global warming.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: Most of the country is just 1.5 metres above sea level with a highest point of 2.3 metres!

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: Many predictions have been made with respect to Maldives being swept away by the rising water level in the Indian Ocean.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: It was even seen during the tsunami of 2004, that many of the island's dry parts were flooded by waters shrinking the island.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The government of the Maldives has begun to purchase land from nearby countries in case the islands go under water!

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: In order to highlight the threats of global warming to its low lying islands, the government of Maldives held a cabinet Underwater meeting underwater in 2009.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: That was the first ever cabinet meeting in the world that took place underwater.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: The meeting took place about 5 meter underwater, in a blue green lagoon on a small island.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Maldives
passages.text: While underwater, the cabinet signed a document calling on all nations to cut their carbon emissions.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: India is our closet neighbour.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: It is the largest among South Asian Countries.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: In fact, India is the seventh largest country in the world with an area of 3,287,590 square kilometres.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: India is bounded by the Indian Ocean on the South, the Arabian Sea on the West and the Bay of Bengal on the East.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: It is bordered by Pakistan to the West; China, Nepal, and Bhutan to the North; and Bangladesh and Myanmar to the East.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: India is the world's second most populous country after China.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: Its current population as in 2010 is around 1.15 billion.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: New Delhi is the capital of India and about 13 million people live in the capital.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: India is a land of ancient civilization.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: The social, economic, and cultural configurations of this vast country are the products of a long process of region expansion.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: Indian history begins with the birth of the Indus Valley Civilization and the coming of the Aryans.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: During this period, Aryan culture flourished in this part of the world.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: The fifth century saw the unification of India under Ashoka, and it is in his time that Buddhism spread in many parts of Asia.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: In the eighth century, Islam came to India for the first time and by the eleventh century it had firmly established itself.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: I resulted into the formation of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 by Qutb ud din Aybek.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: This was finally succeeded by the Mughal Empire in 1526, under which India once again achieved a large measure of political unity.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: It was in the 17th century that the Europeans came to India.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: This coincided with the disintegration of the Mughal Empire, paving the way for supremacy among the English, the French, the Dutch and the Portuguese.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: The English emerged as the 'victors'.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: In 1774 Warren Hastings was appointed the first Governor General of India by the East India Company.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: In 1876 Queen Victoria was given the title Empress of India by the British parliament and India came under the British rule completely.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: They ruled India for nearly two hundred years.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: This period was marked by India's struggle for independence.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: Through a series of heroic and patriotic movements to restore freedom, India got its independence in 1947.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: The culture of India is one of the oldest and unique in the world.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: In India, there is amazing cultural diversity throughout the country.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: The South, North, and Northeast have their own distinct cultures and almost every state has carved out its own cultural distinction.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: There is hardly any culture in the world that is as varied and unique as India.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: There are 17 major languages and 844 dialects used by the people of India.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: India is a tourists' delight.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: The Taj ahal, FatehPur Sikri, the Qutab Minar and the Red Fort are a few of the many wonders which attract people from all over the world.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: Kashmir has been described as a paradise on earth.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: The country of mountains, valleys, deserts, rivers

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: and lakes offer the richness of a mini world within a single country.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: India: Unity within diversity
passages.text: Ooty, Nilgiris and the temples of South India.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Read the following text and answer the questions.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Bhutan is called the Jewel of the Eastern Himalayas.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: This small, landlocked country is located along the southern slopes of the Himalayan range, bounded by Tibet in the North and India from the other sides.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: The official name of Bhutan is Druk yul which means ‘land of the thunder dragon’.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: It earned this name because of the fierce storms That often roll in from the Himalayas.The country has an of 38,394 and a population of China 716,896 Since it is cut off from the rest of the world by the Great Himalayas a unique culture and tradition based on gentle Buddhist beliefs have evolved over time.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Bhutanese men wear Gho - a knee length robe - and women wear Kira - a sheet like cloth piece.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Bhutanese houses are built from mud and stone, with wooden shingle roof.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: The Bhutanese never use iron nails in their buildings.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Usually, the Bhutanese build each other's houses by exchanging labour within the community.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Different Festivals are celebrated all year round in Bhutan.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Colourful masks are used in the festivals which reflect the rich Bhutanese culture.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Dances are performed by the Buddhist monks to protect the valleys and ward off evil spirits.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: The main religious festival is called Tshechus .The teachings of Lord Buddha are enacted through mask dances for three five days in the courtyard of the monasteries.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: People attend these events in their best clothes, with picnic baskets.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Another major festival is called Losar.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: It is celebrated on Lunar New Year.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: People cook special dishes and wear new clothes.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: It is a time for family get -together.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Men play archery or darts while women sing and dance.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Pure mountain air, crystal blue skies and tine vegetation cover have made this small country an ideal destination for the environment lovers.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: The ecosystem of this small nation supports the existence of rich flora and fauna which are protected by strict laws.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Even, anyone found guilty of killing a black-necked crane could be sentenced to life in prison.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: The government of Bhutan has taken a number of steps to protect its bio-diversity.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Photo of A Bhutanese family in traditional clothes

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Bhutan is the first country in the world with specific constitutional obligations on its people to protect the environment.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: As per the constitution, at least 60 percent of the country must remain under forest cover at all times.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Efforts are also taken to protect the nation against the intrusion of foreign cultures and values.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: The first foreign tourists were allowed into Bhutan in 1974.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Now, tourism is encouraged but is controlled and limited to about 6,000 visitors a year.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Bhutan is one of the last countries in the world to introduce television and the Internet to its people.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: The government lifted a ban on TV and the Internet only in 1999.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: The Bhutanese government has made it mandatory for all Bhutanese to wear only their national dress in public.

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: Finally, the most interesting fact about Bhutan is that they are the only country that measures success in Gross National Happiness rather than Gross National Product!

passages.heading: Lesson 5: Bhutan: The land of happiness
passages.text: In 2006, Business Week rated Bhutan as the happiest country in Asia and the eighth happiest country in the world.

passages.text: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: A. Read the text and answer the questions that follow.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: The pioneer of Bangladeshi modern art Zainul Abedin is widely acclaimed for his Bengal `Famine Sketches'.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: Through a series of sketches, Zainul not only documented the harsh famine of 1940 but also showed its sinister face through the skeletal figures of the people destined to die of starvation in a man-made plight.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He depicted these extremely shocking pictures with human compassion.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He made his own ink by burning charcoal and using cheap ordinary packing paper for sketching.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He produced a series of brush and ink drawings, which later became iconic images of human sufferings.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: Zainul developed a knack for drawing and painting when he was a high school student.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: After completing high school, he got admission to the Government School of Art, Calcutta (now Kolkata).

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He graduated with the first position in first class in 1938.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He was appointed teacher of the Art School while he was still a student there.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He also attended the Slade School of Arts, London in 1951-52.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: Zainul Abedin is considered the founding father of Bangladeshi art.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He was an artist of outstanding talent and earned international reputation.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: For his artistic and visionary qualities, he is referred to as Shilpacharya meaning `great teacher of art' in Bangladesh.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He was the first Principal of the first art school in Dhaka in East Pakistan (now Bangladesh).

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He organized the Nabanna (harvest) exhibition in 1969.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: In the exhibition, a 65-foot long scroll portraying the rural East Pakistan in phases from abundance to poverty.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: This intensified the already heightened non-cooperation movement against the Pakistan regime.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: The exhibition was symbolic of the artists' protest and a milestone in demanding cultural and political freedom.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: Zainul's dynamic style of work is evident in a 30 foot long scroll painting called Manpura, which was done to commemorate the death of hundreds and thousands of people in the devastating cyclone of 1970.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He designed the pages of Constitution of Bangladesh.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: He founded the Folk Art Museum at Sonargoan, and also Zainul Abedin Shangrahasala, a gallery of his own works in Mymensingh in 1975.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: The river Brahmaputra played a vital role in his paintings and was a source of inspiration all through his career.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: Much of his childhood was spent near the scenic beauty of the river Brahmaputra.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: A series of water colours that Zainul did as his tribute to the river earned him the Governor's Gold Medal in an all-India exhibition in 1938.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: This was the first time when he came into spotlight and this award gave him the confidence to create his own visual style.

passages.heading: Lesson l: Zainul Abedin, the great artist
passages.text: Zainul was born in Kishoreganj on 29 December 1914 and died on 28 May 1976.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: In the primitive age communications took place between humans through signs and gestures.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: As humans began to use their vocal chords, these silent gestures were no longer used as the primary means of communication.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: But they did not completely disappear.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: They evolved as a form of art, used to entertain thousands, and came to be Known as 'mime'.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Mime touched a little boy's heart while he was watching a performance in his village.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: He was so fascinated by the show that he was determined to master this art.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: He is no other than Partha Pratim Majumder.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: partha is undoubtedly a forerunner in the field of mime in Bangladesh.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: He started as a musician and his keen sense of rhythm helped him to let his limbs move and express his surroundings through gestures.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Partha Pratim Majumder is the first Bangladeshi to take up mime as a profession.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: He performed in a number of television shows in Bangladesh and gained popularity.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: In his mime, Majumder depicted the day-to-day life of the people.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: There were sadness, tears as well as happiness and laughter.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Miajumder's turning point of life came in 1979, when he was asked to give a solo performance in Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: The then French ambassador Loic Moreau happened to be among the audience.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Mr.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Moreau noticed the talent in Majumder.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: In 1981, the French Government offered him a scholarship so that he could get professional training in mime.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: This was the first time that a student was granted a French scholarship in mime.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Majumder started his training under the legendry maestro, Etiene Decroux.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Through Decroux, he met another celebrated mime artist named Marcel Marceau.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Marceau has transformed modern mime by taking it to an unimaginable height.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: Marceau was very impressed by the Bangladeshi young talent and offered him a place in his school for mime, named `Ecole Internationale de Mimodrame de Paris-Marcel Marceau' This school of mime is the biggest and the best in the world.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: During his three years training period, Majumder practiced 16-18 hours daily till each and every bone in his body would feel like breaking.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: After his time with Marceau, there was no looking back for Majumder.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: He staged solo performances in England; Belgium, Germany, Spain, Italy and the USA.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: French, Canadian and American TV channels enthusiastically aired his shows.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: In 2009, for his role in the popular French drama Majumder won the " Moliere Award" which is the highest distinction in the French Theatre.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: As a pioneer of the art of mime in Bangladesh and for popularizing the artistic genre, Bangladesh Government honoured the artiste with the highest award of the country called "Ekuslley Padok" in 2010.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The art of silence
passages.text: The Government of France has also honoured him for his contribution to the art of mime throughout the world with the highest cultural award of France titled "Chevalier de I'odre des Arts et des Lettres" (Knight in the order of Arts and Literature) in the year 2011.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: She was the youngest of the three siblings and was named Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: Who had known that this tiny, little girl would one day become the servant of humanity- would love and serve the poorest of the poor and become the mother of humanity.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: Yes, we are talking about none other than Mother Teresa.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: At the age of 12, she heard a voice from within her that urged her to spread the love of Christ.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: She decided that she would be a missionary.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: At the age of 18 she left her parental home.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: She then joined an Irish community of nuns called the Sisters of Loreto, which had missions in India.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: After a few months of training at the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Dublin, Mother Teresa came to India.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: On May 24, 1931, she took her initial vows as a nun.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: From 1931 to 1948, Mother Teresa taught geography and theology at St.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: Mary's High School in Kolkata (then Calcutta).

passages.heading: Lesson 4: The beginning
passages.text: However, the prevailing poverty in Kolkata had a deep impact on Mother Teresa's mind, and in 1948 she received permission from her superiors to leave the convent and devote herself to work among the poorest of the poor in the slums of Kolkata.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Mother Teresa was moved by the presence of the sick and dying on the streets of Kolkata.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: She founded the home for the dying destitute and named it `Nirmal Hridoy', meaning `Pure Heart'.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: She and her fellow nuns gathered the dying people off the streets of Kolkata and brought them to this home.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: They were lovingly looked after and cared for.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Since then men, women and children have been taken from the streets and carried to Nirmol Hridoy.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: These unloved and uncared for people get an opportunity to die in an environment of kindness and love.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: In their last hours they get human and Divine love, and can feel they are also children of God.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: The Missionaries of Charity try to find jobs for those who survive, or send them to homes where they can live happily for some more years in a caring environment.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Regarding commitment to family, Mother Teresa said, " Maybe in our own family, we have somebody, who is feeling lonely, who is feeling sick, who is feeling worried.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Are we there?

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Are we willing to give until it hurts in order to be with our families, or do we put our interest first?

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: We must remember that love begins at home and we must also remember that future of humanity passes through the family".

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Mother Teresa's work has been recognized throughout the world and she has received a number of awards.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: These include the Pope John XXIII Peace Prize (1971), the Nehru Prize for Promotion of International Peace & Understanding (1972), the Balzan Prize (1978), the Nobel Peace Prize (1979) and the Bharat Ratna (1980).

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Mother Teresa died at the age of 87, on 5 September 1997.The world salutes her for her love and compassion for humanity.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: She has taught us how to extend our hand towards those who need our love and support irrespective of creed, caste and religion.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Draped in a white and blue-bordered sari, wrinkled face, ever soft eyes and a saintly smile is the picture of Mother Teresa in our mind.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Steven Paul Jobs ( 24 February 1955 - 5 October 2011) , most popularly known as Steve Jobs was the co-founder, chairman and chief executive officer of Apple Inc.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: He was the pioneer of the personal computer revolution.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: He was famous for his career the electronic field of computers and consumers.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: This became possible through marketing of Apple computers.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: In 1985, Jobs Left Apple after losing a power battle with the board of directors.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: He then founded NeXT, a computer platform development company specializing in the higher education and business market.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: On the other hand, Apple failed to bring up any new operating system during Job's absence.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Jobs returned to Apple as an adviser, and took control of the company as an interim CEO.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: By 1998, Jobs brought back Apple to profitability from the verge of bankruptcy.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: He supervised the development of iMac iTunes, iPod, iPhone and iPad.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: These devices are so simple and user friendly that even a child can operate them.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: He supervised the company's Apple Stores, iTunes Store and the App Store too.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: The success of these products and services brought about steady financial returns for several years and pushed Apple to become the world's most valuable publicly traded company in 2011.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: This triumph is regarded as the greatest turnarounds in the business history.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Steve Jobs has been highly acclaimed as a visionary leader.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: He has changed people's -perspective computer, and how they use it, consume personal media, and how they communicate with each other.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Hence i-Books, i-Phones, i-Pods and i-Pads have become extremely popular.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Jobs saw and felt the need of Wi-Fi (wireless internet connection) in laptops.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: It is he who made Wi-Fi a standard feature of every laptop, and of many other devices worldwide.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: So Jobs dream to be anywhere anytime became a reality.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: Jobs also co-founded and served as chief executive of Pixar Animation Studios.

passages.heading: Lesson 6: Love for humanity
passages.text: He became a member of the board of directors of The Walt Disney Company in 2006, when Disney acquired Pixar.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: A car mechanic Paul Jobs and his wife Clara jobs adopted Steve who was abandoned at birth.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: Paul and Clara loved Steve very much.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: They made him feel that he was `chosen' and very `special'.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: One of his colleagues, Del Yocam said about Steve, "I think his desire for complete control of whatever he makes derives directly from his personality and from the fact that he was abandoned at birth."

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: Jobs' mother taught him how to read and write before he went to the elementary school.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: So when he went to school, he found out that he knew everything that the teachers were teaching.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: He got bored and played pranks to keep himself busy.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: This continued for the first few years.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: It was clear from his behaviour that he could not accept other people's authority.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: He said, "I encountered authority of a different kind that I have never encountered before, and I did not like it."

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: A turning point came when he was in grade four.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: His teacher Imogene Hill watched him very closely for some time and soon found out how to handle him and get things done by him.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: In order to get things done she used to give him money and food.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: One day after school, she gave Jobs a workbook with math problems in it.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: She said, " I want you to take it home and do this."

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: She showed Jobs a huge lollipop and said, " When you are done with it, if you get it mostly right, I will give you this and five dollar”.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: Within two days, Job solved the math and returned the book to his teacher

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: This continued for a couple of months and Jobs enjoyed learning so much that he did not need any return.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: Also he liked his teacher very much and wanted to please her.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: In Ms.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: Hill's class, Jobs felt he was special.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: At the end of the fourth grade, Jobs did very well.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: It was clear not only to Jobs and his parents but also to the teachers that he was exceptionally intelligent.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: The school proposed that Jobs should skip two classes and go into seventh grade.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: This would mean that Jobs would find the study challenging and he would be motivated to study.

passages.heading: Lesson 8: Jobs' childhood
passages.text: His parents had him skip only one grade.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: ‘Heritage’ is what we inherit from the past, live with them in the present and then pass on to our children or future generation.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: Our unique source of life and inspiration is our cultural and natural heritage.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: When we speak of `World Heritage', it indicates places and sites that we got from the past and pass on to the future generation of the entire world.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The `Shat Gambuj Mosque' in Bagerhat is such a heritage.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: Originally, the historic Mosque City was known as ` Khalifatabad'.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: It is situated at the outskirts of Bagerhat town--- not very far from the dense mangrove forest of the Sundarbans.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: Khalifatabad was a Muslim colony.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: It was founded by the Turkish general, a saint warrior Ulugh Khan Jahan in the 15th century.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The infrastructure of the city reveals significant technical skills in many mosques as well as early Islamic monuments.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: Baked bricks were used for the construction of the buildings.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The planning of the city was distinctly dominated by Islamic architecture and the decorations were a combination of Mughal and Turkish architecture.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: Khan Jahan built a network of roads, bridges, public buildings and reservoirs to make the city habitable.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: There were about 360 mosques in the city.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: Among them the most remarkable is the multi-domed Shat Gombuj Mosque.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The mosque is unique in the sense that it has 60 pillars that support the roof, with 77 low height domes.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The 4 towers at 4 comers have smaller domes on the roof as well.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The vast prayer hall has 11 arched doorways on the east and 7 each on the north and south for light and ventilation.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: It has 7 aisles running along the length of the mosque and 11deep curves between the slender stone columns.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: These columns support the curving arches created by the domes.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The thickness of the arches is 6 feet and have slightly narrowing hollow and round wall.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The west wall in the interior has 11 ‘mihrabs’ (niche in mosque pointing towards Mskkah).

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: These mihrabs are decorated with stonework and terracotta.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: The floor of the mosque is made of brick.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: Besides being used as a prayer hall, Khan Jahan used the mosque as his court also.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: The Shat Gambuj Mosque
passages.text: Today, it is one of the greatest tourist attractions and one of the best architectural beauties of Bangladesh.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Paharpur is an important archaeological site situated in a village named `Paharpur' in Naogaon district of northern Bangladesh.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Naogoan is mainly plain land but in the middle of it stood a hill covered with jungle.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: When the jungle was cleared and the hill excavated, there emerged a lofty ruin of an ancient temple.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The temple is about 24 metre high from the surrounding level.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: `Pahar' means hill.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Hence is the name Paharpur.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The Paharpur site has been excavated and re-excavated a number of times by archaeologists.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Sir Alexander visited the place in 1879.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Cunningham intended to carry out an extensive excavation but was prevented by the land owner.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Nevertheless, he was satisfied with whatever excavation he was permitted to carry on.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: He discovered the ruins of a square tower of 22 feet side with a projection in the middle of each side from the top of the central hill.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The site was declared to be protected by the Archaeological Survey of India in 1919 under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act of 1904.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Systematic and regular excavation started jointly by Archaeological Survey of India, and Varendra Research Society of Rajshahi and Kolkata ( at that time known as Calcutta) University in 1923.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: They excavated the south-west corner of the monastery.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Next in 1925-26, R D Banerjee excavated the northern part of the central mound.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: From 1926-27 onward, excavation was carried out under the supervision of KN Dikshit.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The Department of Archaeology of Bangladesh brought the site under further excavation after independence.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The operations took place in two phases.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The first phase was initiated in 1981-82 and continued to 1984-1985.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The second phase was started in 1988-89 and continued to 1990-91.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Pre-liberation expeditions have revealed the architectural remains of a vast Buddhist monastery, the Somapura Mahavihara.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: It is dominated by the central shrine, attracting immediate attention by its lofty height and unusual architectural design.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Somapura Mahavihara was one of the most famous Buddhist institutions for monks of ancient Bengal and in southern Asia.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The excavated complex at Paharpur has been identified with the Somapura Mahavihara built by the second Pala king Dharmapala (781-821 AD).

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Some clay seals from the ruins bear the inscription Shri-Somapure- Shri-Dharmapaladeva-Mahavihariyarya-bhiksu.szi-sangghasya.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: The Pala rulers were devout Buddhists and they founded a number of monasteries throughout their growing empire.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: The Somapura Mahavihara
passages.text: Some of them became great centres of learning and their reputation quickly spread throughout Asia.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The French Sculptor Frederic Auguste Bartholdi was assigned to design and complete a sculpture within 1876, so that it could be a gift for the Americans on the occasion of celebrating the hundred years of the American Declaration of Independence.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The statue was a joint venture between the USA and France.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The French people would build the statue and assemble it in the States, and the people of the USA were to build the pedestal for the statue.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: Raising money for the pedestal was completed in August 1885.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The construction of the pedestal was finished in April 1886.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: In the meantime, France completed the Statue in July 1884.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: They sent it to New York on board the French war ship `Isere' in 1885.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: While transporting the statue, it was split up into 350 individual pieces and packed in 214 crates.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: It took four months to put the Statue together and place it on the pedestal.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: Thousands of people saw the unveiling ceremony of the Statue of Liberty on October 28th 1886.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: It was centennial gift ten years late.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The Freedom that the Statue stands for is not stationary.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The broken chain wrapped around her feet, sticking out from the bottom of her robe, symbolizes her free forward movement, enlightening the world with her torch, free from oppression and slavery.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The Statue's original torch was the first part constructed in 1876.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: It was replaced by a new copper torch covered in 24K gold leaf in 1984.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The torch is lighted by flood light at night.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The original torch is currently located in the lobby of the monument.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: Access to the torch has been closed since 1916.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: From October 28, 2011, on her 125th anniversary, the Statue of Liberty was named Liberty Enlightening the World wide Web".

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The credit goes to a series of new web cams placed around her torch.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: Several amazing views will be just a click of a mouse away.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: On clear days, three cameras provide unobstructed scenes and views.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: Two cameras provide an ultra-wide-angle interactive view of the famous golden torch.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: The remaining camera looks downwards towards the crown of The Statue of Liberty, her face, the tablet she is holding from your computer or smart phone.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: The Statue of Liberty
passages.text: So a person can have access to the web cam's live feed of The Statue of Liberty from anywhere in the world.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal
passages.text: The average water level in the lake is never higher than 456m.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal
passages.text: The average depth of Lake Baikal is 730 m., and its maximum depth in the middle is 1,620 m.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal
passages.text: It would take about one year for all the rivers of the world to fill Baikal's basin, and would take four hundred years for all the rivers, streams and brooks now flowing into Siberian lake sea to do the same.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal
passages.text: Baikal is a stormy lake.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal
passages.text: But if the winds get stronger, Baikal turns black, waves rising high with white crest.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: Lake Baikal

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Read the text. It is about a young entrepreneur, Sayeed Kamal Notice what he thinks about job and happiness. Then answer the questions that follow.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I know you will wonder if I say the best thing that ever happened to me was when I lost my last job.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Yes, really!

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I was a desk clerk in an office.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: But believe me I never liked my job.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Nothing can be more boring than being stuck in an office all day with computers and telephone.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: So after two years or so, I decided to leave my job though I had good salary there.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Now I'm an owner of a nursery.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Planting seeds, budding, grafting, taking care of saplings, cleaning the flower beds and spending time with trees are my full time job.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I start work very early.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: In summer I usually leave home at 5:30 in the morning, but in winter not until about 7.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I've a small hut in my nursery.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: There cannot be any more pleasure for me than when I see the moon from there or walk through the trees in the soft moonlit night.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: The winter is just over.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: So I'm cleaning up the winter flower garden.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Now I'm busy in producing more timber and medicinal plants which people will buy from July.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Every season is so different and I love them all.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: When I compare my present days with the past, I simply can't understand how I could survive there in my previous job.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I love nature.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I just love working outside in the open air after all those months in a stuffy office.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Gadgets never attract me and perhaps never will.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I'm not married.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I do my own work, even cook my own food.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I try not to depend on others for the work which I myself can do.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Often my friends are annoyed with me.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: They say, I should engage a maid for household chores.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: They are not happy to see me in this `rustic life'.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: They are professionals.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: They earn a lot.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Maybe --- much more than what I do but I think I enjoy my work more.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: At weekends, I often go to the countryside.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Sometimes with my friends, sometimes alone.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I love collecting unknown saplings.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I have another hobby.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I love collecting stamps.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I have a Russian stamp during the period of Lenin.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I don't watch TV Almost everyone has a TV set these days.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: But I don't have any.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: How is that?

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: The only problem I face is I do not earn enough money in all seasons.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: The winter and the rain are two busy seasons for me.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: But it's OK.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: Maybe I do not earn enough like many other people around me.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: But I at least earn enough for my family, employees, and me to run a decent life.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Jobs around
passages.text: I must say I'm a very happy man!

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Read the text and answer the following questions.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: What type of job do you want to have?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Is it a highly paid and high-profile conventional job liked by most people?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Yes, you can have it.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: It is the question of your choice and important decisions that would help you to advance your life ahead.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: But have you ever thought of other types of jobs out there--- cool, fun, exciting, even strange or weird jobs you never imagined to exist?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: What are they?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Did you ever wonder who picks up the chewing gum left on a park bench or who assesses whether a piece of furniture is comfortable enough or who constructs glass eyeballs or who farms oysters in the middle of the ocean?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: These are all wacky, odd, unexpected, wild, crazy, unconventional, strange or just plain weird jobs and careers.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: They are not your traditional career choices, but somebody out there does all these things, gets paid for it, and enjoys life like anybody else.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: There are hundreds of such jobs to take if you want to travel the less taken ways of life.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: You have to decide on several questions:

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: What companies will recruit/hire me?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Do I actually make a paycheck?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: What type of education/diploma will I need?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Can I make a living doing this?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Your answers to these questions will help pave your career roadmap and help you decide if you are ready to take the challenge.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Decide if you want a change.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: A lot of strange jobs also allow you to work part-time or freelance when it fits your schedule.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: This way you can get a taste of freedom, a secondary income and build experience at the same time.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Do you have interests beyond writing memos and attending boring meetings?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: If so, you may wonder how you can find a strange job.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Hobbies are a good place to start.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: You may enjoy it.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Someone out there works in that field and is making money off their hobby.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: Maybe they are testing mountaineering equipment, developing fragrances, trying new brands of undergarments, or saving sea turtles.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Weird jobs around
passages.text: And they are getting paid good wages.

passages.text: They are also known as florists and they create superb arrangements with flowers.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: Using both real and artificial flowers with other greeneries, florists prepare flower displays for a variety of events such as weddings, birthdays, anniversaries, marriage days, Valentine's day, official receptions and even funerals.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: Every flower is with its distinct colour, design, significance and meaning which flower designers have to know well.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: There are conventions and significance associated with flowers.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: We know that conventionally roses are meant for romance and anniversaries and tulips for birthdays.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: Although formal education or a diploma is not always essential, florists must have a good taste, good eye for colours, shapes and proportion.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: They have to have good sense for selecting flowers, ribbons and other accessories to make beautiful arrangements.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: Professional florists are knowledgeable about not only flowers but also designs and techniques.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: Most florists learn the trade mainly through apprenticeship in a previous flower farming job and also by attending formal floral schools and courses.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: However, a true passion for flowers and a bit of aesthetic sense are all that can make a florist's career successful.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: Flower designers earn fairly handsome money.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: But the bonus is that they belong to a fresh fun job.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: They work in flowers all day long in a nice atmosphere with fresh air, pleasant smells and vivid colours around.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: But there is a disadvantage too, if you are inclined to see so.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Floral career
passages.text: Florists deal with flowers, but miss their honey!

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: Pritilata was born in Chittagong on 5 May 1911.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: She was a meritorious student at Dr Khastagir Government Girls' School in Chittagong and Eden College, Dhaka.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: She finally graduated in philosophy with distinction from Bathune College in Kolkata.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: In her college days, Pritilata was an activist in the anti-British movement.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: All through her life, she dreamt of two things: a society without gender discrimination, and her motherland without British colonial rule.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: So she received combat training to fight against the British rule.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: Soon after, Pritilata became the head teacher of Nandankanon Aparna Charan School in Chittagong.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: Gradually she involved herself in Surja Sen's armed resistance movement.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: Surja Sen was a famous anti-British movement organizer and activist in Chittagong area that time.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: In 1932, Surja Sen planned an attack on the Pahartali European Club.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: The club was well-known for its notorious sign Dogs and Indians not allowed.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: Surya Sen assigned Pritilata to lead a team of 10-12 men to attack the Club.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: The raid was successful but Pritilata dressed as a man failed to get out of the Club.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: She committed suicide by taking potassium cyanide to avoid arrest.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: She proved that women can work like men.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: She also proved that women too needed to be prepared to sacrifice their lives for the freedom from the British colonial rule.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: Her dream came true.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: They had dreams 1
passages.text: The British rule came to an end though she couldn't Pahartali European Club see it during her lifetime.

passages.text: Read the text.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: Zahir Raihan was one of the most talented film makers in Bangladesh.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: He was born on 19 August 1935 in the village Majupur, in Feni district.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: He was an active worker of the Language Movement.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: He was one of the ten students to go out in a procession on 21 February 1952 despite a ban on such activities.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: As a result, he and many others were arrested and taken to prison.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: Zahir was also present at the historical meeting of Amtala on February 21, 1952.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: He also took part in the mass movement in 1969.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: In 1971, he joined the Liberation War.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: All through his life, Zahir dreamt for a democratic society, a society that will ensure freedom of speech and will.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: He had many dreams about our film industry too.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: He made a legendary film Jibon Theke Neya based on the Language Movement of 1952.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: It was a revolt against the then autocratic government.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: The family presented in that film was a miniature East Pakistan ruled by an autocrat who had to go to the prison for her conspiracy.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: During the liberation war this film was shown outside Bangladesh.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: Critics like Satyajit Ray, Mrinal Sen, and Ritwik Ghatak appreciated this film.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: Zahir gave all his money to the Freedom Fighters' trust that he got from his film shows.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: Besides, his great documentary on Pakistani atrocities, Stop Genocide, helped create world sentiment in favour of our liberation war.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: On 30 December 1971, someone informed Zahir about an address somewhere at Mirpur, where he might find his brother, the famous writer Shahidullah Kaiser.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: Shahidulla was captured and killed by the Pakistani army and the local collaborators during the last days of the war.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: Accordingly, Zahir left home to get his brother back and he never returned.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: Zahir's dream was fulfilled.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: He could see the inception of a free independent Bangladesh though he did not get back his brother.

passages.heading: Lesson 4: They had dreams 2
passages.text: And it's a pity that this dreamer was missing at such a time when his dream came true.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: Sohan lives in a village in the south-west part of Bangladesh.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: Last night he could not sleep.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: His sister had the SSC exam next morning.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: She could not read either.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: There was load-shedding.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: The summer night being sticky hot, life became hell without electricity.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: Most of their area remained dark for hours due to power shortage.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: In May-June, temperature shoots up to 40 degree Celsius.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: With almost 90 percent of humidity in the atmosphere, it becomes all sweat, wet, damp and stinky.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: When you are busy fanning yourself all the time, how can you concentrate on studies?

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: In the night it is impossible to sit in the study with a candle light or table lamp or hurricane lamp or a rural kerosene lamp.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: People simply come out of houses almost bare-bodied and sit in the open places.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: Some splash cold water on their faces.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: Fans are still; lamps are out and it is dark everywhere.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: It is simply unbearable.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: What is the reason of frequent load-shedding?

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: Press reports say there is a shortage in electricity production.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: According to the Power development authorities, the demand for electricity a few years ago was more than 6,000 MW* a day while the supply remained around 4,200 MW In the rural areas, the Rural Electrification Board (REB) could supply barely half of the total demand which was around 2,400 MW per day.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: In the capital city, the demand stood at around 1,400 MW while the supply amounted to 650 MW.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: As a result, load-shedding is unavoidable for the time being.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: But situation is improving very fast.

passages.heading: Lesson 1: Renewable energy sources -1
passages.text: *MW is Mega Watt which is the unit to measure electricity

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: In a speech at the 90th Science Congress, internationally acknowledged scientist and former Indian president Mr APJ Abdul Kalam mentioned a very important aspect of mankind's future energy crisis.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: He pointed out that the era of wood and bio-mass has almost come to an end.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: The age of oil and natural gas would soon be over within the next few decades.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: Massive burning of world's coal reserves may lead to a worldwide ecological disaster because coal burning emits the highest amount of carbon in the atmosphere.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: Ukraine's (former Soviet Union) Chernobyl disaster in 1986 has exposed that nuclear energy can be potentially dangerous too.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: So according to Kalam, the only solution that mankind can look to is the massive use of solar energy in future because . it has some advantages over other forms of renewable energies.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: Now why has Kalam put so much importance to the issue of energy?

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: The energy sources have always been a major factor of change throughout history.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: The world's petroleum consumption has increased from annually 3 billion barrels in 1930 to annually 50 billion barrels today.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: In the next quarter century, the world's population is expected to be about 8 billion which is 30 percent higher than today.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: Developing countries will grow their economies about two times faster than industrialized countries.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: Global economic growth is expected to continue at 3 percent per year.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: Consequently, the global demand for energy will grow at about 1.7 percent per year on an average.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: It indicates a 50-percent rise of energy consumption by 2030.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: If the world's daily petroleum consumption is 220 million barrels now, it will rise to 335 million barrels by that time.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: The present reserve of hydro-carbon energy resources is limited and it will not be sufficient to meet the future energy challenges of the world.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: And hence, leading industrial countries have taken initiatives to tap alternative energy sources mainly known as green or renewable energy sources.

passages.heading: Lesson 2: Renewable energy sources -2
passages.text: The bottom line of Kalam's speech indicates that concern of mankind in the 21 St the century.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Read the text and answer the following questions.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Countries of the world rely heavily on petroleum, coal and natural gas for their energy sources.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: There are two major types of energy sources: renewable and non-renewable.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Hydro-carbon or fossil fuels are non-renewable sources of energy.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Reliance on them poses real big problems.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: First, fossil fuels such as oil, coal, gas etc, are finite energy resources and the world eventually will run out of them.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Secondly, they will become too expensive in the coming decades and too damaging for the environment to repair.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Thirdly, fossil fuels have direct polluting impacts on earth's environment causing global warming.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: In contrast, renewable energy sources such as, wind and solar energy are constantly and naturally replenished and never run out.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Most renewable energy comes either directly or indirectly from the sun.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Sunlight or solar energy can be used for heating and lighting homes, for generating electricity and for other commercial and industrial uses.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: The sun's heat drives the wind and this wind energy can be captured with wind turbines to produce electricity.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Then the wind and the sun's heat cause water to evaporate.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: When this water vapour turns into rain or snow and flows downhill into rivers or streams, its energy can be captured as hydroelectric energy.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Along with the rain and snow, sunlight causes plants to grow.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Plants produce biomass which again can be turned into fuels such as fire wood, alcohol, etc. identified as bioenergy.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Scientists have identified Hydrogen as another form of renewable energy source.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: It is the most abundant element in nature.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: But it does not exist separately as a gas.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: It is always combined with other elements, such as with oxygen to make water.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Hydrogen, separated from another element, can be burned as a fuel to produce electricity.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Our Earth's interior contains molten lava with tremendous heat.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: This heat inside the Earth produces steam and hot water which can be tapped as geothermal energy to produce electricity, for heating homes, etc.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Ocean energy comes from several sources.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: Ocean's force of tide and wave can be used to produce energy.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: The surface of the ocean gets more heat from the sun than the ocean depths.

passages.heading: Lesson 3: Renewable energy sources-3
passages.text: This temperature difference can be used as energy source too.
